product.title: Uzbek 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Uzbek: short dialogues, word-for-word translations that show how Uzbek builds its sentences, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises, and an answer key. Uzbek is friendlier than it looks: it uses the Latin alphabet, its spelling is almost perfectly regular, its nouns have no gender, and it has no articles. Each unit targets one real stumbling block, from the verb that always waits at the end of the sentence to the ending -ni that appears only when the object is specific.

blocks.text: Uzbek is the language of Samarkand, Bukhara, and the Silk Road cities — and of more than 35 million people today. It's also far more approachable than its reputation. Open any page of this course and you'll find words that have traveled the world: *kitob* (book, Arabic *kitab*), *bozor* (bazaar), *shakar* (sugar), *safar* (journey, as in *safari*), *choy* (tea, *chai*), *dunyo* (world), *rahmat* (thank you), *salom* (hello).

Uzbek is a Turkic language, a close relative of Turkish, Kazakh, and Uyghur. Over the centuries it absorbed hundreds of words from Arabic and Persian, and in the twentieth century a layer of Russian. If you know any of those languages, you'll recognize a lot. If you don't, you still start with more than you think.

The first gift: **the Latin alphabet**. Since 1993 Uzbek has officially been written with the same letters you are reading right now. There's no new script to learn first, no three months spent learning to spell. The very first page of this course goes straight into sentences.

The second gift, and the biggest relief: **Uzbek nouns have no gender**. No *der/die/das*, no *le/la*, no adjectives that change to match the noun. Even "he" and "she" are one word, *u*. There are no articles either — no *a*, no *the*. And if you've heard that Turkish has tricky vowel harmony, here's good news: modern Uzbek **has almost entirely dropped it**. One ending, one form. *-da* is always *-da*, whatever vowels the word has.
So where's the difficulty? In three places, and none of them is about memorizing.

First, **the verb stands at the end of the sentence**. "I read a book" becomes *Men kitob oʻqiyman* — "I book read". Every long sentence makes you hold the verb back until the end, and in the first week that feels like walking backward.

Second, **Uzbek prepositions come after the word, as endings**. Not "at home" but *uy-da*, not "to the bazaar" but *bozor-ga*, not "from Jakarta" but *Jakarta-dan*. Six endings do the work of almost all the prepositions you use every day.

Third, **the ending -ni, which comes and goes**. *Men kitob oʻqiyman* means "I read books (any book)"; *Men kitobni oʻqiyman* means "I'm reading the book (the one we both know)". English shows this with *a* and *the*; Uzbek has no articles, so it marks the specific object with an ending. It has to become a new habit — which is why all of unit 7 is devoted to it.
None of these three is put off until the end. Word order is set up in unit 6, the place endings come in units 4 and 8, and *-ni* gets a whole unit to itself.
The explanations are short on purpose. What's long isn't the theory but the practice.

blocks.title: Before you start
items: Set aside 20–30 uninterrupted minutes, not two hours broken into pieces. Languages stick through short, frequent repetition, not one long attack.
Read out loud. In Uzbek that costs you little: the spelling is honest, one letter is one sound, and the stress almost always falls on the last syllable.
Pay attention to the two letters with a little tail from day one: **oʻ** and **gʻ**. The tail isn't decoration — *ot* means "horse", *oʻt* means "grass", and they're two completely different words.

Don't wait for your pronunciation to be perfect before you speak. Uzbeks rarely meet foreigners who bother to learn their language; even the smallest effort is welcomed far more warmly than you'd imagine.

blocks.text: Enjoy the journey. *Omad tilayman!* (Good luck!)

front.title: Contents
front.intro: This course works best in order — each unit reuses what the previous ones set up.

blocks.text: This course is designed for **self-study**. Each unit is meant to be finished in one sitting, about 20–30 minutes. What matters isn't how fast you move forward but how often you come back.
Every unit has the same structure, and the order is deliberate:

items: **Dialogue** — first read the Uzbek out loud without looking at the translation. Let your ears work before your brain demands an explanation.

**Word-for-word translation** — the small italic line under the translation. It's the part people skip most often, yet it's where you see how Uzbek *thinks*. For example: *Ismingiz nima?* literally means "name-your what?", and *Menda pul bor* means "at-me money there-is" — not "I have money".
**Notes** — short explanations of whatever felt strange.
**Vocabulary** — the new words of the unit, with a pronunciation guide.
**Exercises** — do them without looking at the key. Mistakes are part of the process.
**Answer key** — open it only after you've really tried.

blocks.title: Spaced review
items: From unit 3 on, each unit asks you to review an earlier unit — usually two steps back, just the right distance to make your memory work without feeling like starting over. It works in reverse: cover the Uzbek, look at the English, and rebuild the Uzbek sentence from memory.
This is what turns "I understood it once" into "I can use it". Don't skip it.

blocks.title: One habit special to this course
items: Every time you meet a new noun, say it with the three place endings at once: *uy* → *uyda*, *uyga*, *uydan*. Ten seconds per word, and the endings that replace English prepositions stop being theory.
Every time you meet a new verb, say it in a whole sentence with the verb at the end. Not *oʻqimoq* on its own, but *Men kitob oʻqiyman*. Uzbek word order is learned with your mouth, not your eyes.

blocks.text: One last rule: **say it out loud**. Uzbek rewards you for it, because the spelling is honest — once you know the six letters that don't sound the way you'd expect, you can read any word correctly, including words you've never seen.

This section is short, and that's the good news. Uzbek is written in a **Latin alphabet** whose spelling is almost completely honest: a letter is always read the same way, in every word. No silent letters, no surprises like in English or French.
Most Uzbek letters sound just as you'd expect. Only **six** need attention, and this whole page is really about those six.
Six tricky letters

head: Letter
Say it
Example
Notes
rows: Not an ordinary "o". It's an "a" said with rounded lips — between *a* and *o*, like the *o* in British *hot* or the *aw* in *law*. The "Say it" column writes it **å**.
This is the one that sounds like a plain "o", as in *more* (without the r). The little tail changes everything.
A rough sound from the throat, like the *ch* in Scottish *loch* or German *Bach*.
The voiced partner of *kh* — like a French *r*, or a soft gargle.
A "k" said far back in the throat, like the *q* in Arabic *Qur'an*. Keep it apart from plain *k*: *qish* (winter) ≠ *kish*.
Always "e" as in *bed* — **never** "ee", and never silent.

blocks.text: The rest fits in one breath: **sh** as in *shop*, **ch** as in *church*, **j** as in *jam*, **y** as in *yes*, and **ng** as in *sing*. The letter **v** is between *v* and *w*; say it like *w* and you won't sound odd. In the "Say it" column, **a** is as in *father* or *cat*, **i** as in *machine* but short, **u** as in *put* or *moon*, and **ai** as in *eye*.
The ʼ mark on its own

Besides the tail on *oʻ* and *gʻ*, a similar mark can stand on its own in the middle of a word: *maʼno* (meaning), *aʼlo* (excellent), *sanʼat* (art). It's called *tutuq belgisi*, and its job is a brief catch in the breath — like the break in the middle of *uh-oh*. Sometimes it simply lengthens the vowel before it.
The stress rule: one sentence

**Stress almost always falls on the last syllable**: *ki-TOB*, *rah-MAT*, *o-ZBEK*, *sa-lo-mat-LIK*. That's why the **Say it** column throughout the course writes the stressed syllable in capitals — it's predictable, but it's kept so your eye gets used to it.

The exceptions are few and easy to remember: the question words *NI-ma* (what), *QA-yer* (where), *QA-non*? — and the question ending *-mi* never pulls the stress away: *o-zbek-MI-siz* keeps the stress on *-mi*, not on *-siz*. Loanwords from Russian keep their original stress: *av-TO-bus*, *ma-GA-zin*.
Pairs that prove the tail matters
In handwriting and on signs, the tail is often written as an ordinary apostrophe: *o'zbek*, *tog'*. You'll see both forms in Uzbekistan, and they mean the same thing.
The Cyrillic you'll still come across

Uzbekistan switched from the Cyrillic to the Latin alphabet in 1993, but the switch isn't completely finished. Shop signs, old newspapers, and older people still use Cyrillic: *Ўзбекистон* = *Oʻzbekiston*. This course uses only the official Latin alphabet — just know that the other one exists, and don't be surprised to see it on the street.
This page isn't for memorizing. It shows that you start this language with more than you think.

Arabic and Persian were once the languages of learning, religion, and trade from Spain to Southeast Asia. Uzbek absorbed them through Samarkand and Bukhara, and some of the same words reached English too (*bazaar*, *sugar*, *safari*, *divan*). If you know Arabic, Persian, Turkish, Urdu, Hindi, Malay, or Indonesian, many of these will look familiar.

blocks.title: ⚠ Six words whose meaning has shifted
items: **kasal** = **SICK**. *Men kasalman* means "I'm sick" — nothing to do with "casual".
**doʻkon** = **SHOP**. From Arabic *dukkān* (stall) — the same word as Turkish *dükkân*, Hindi-Urdu *dukān*.
**maslahat** = **ADVICE**, not "public good" as in Arabic *maṣlaḥa*. *Maslahat bering* = "give me some advice".
**taklif** = **PROPOSAL or INVITATION**, not "burden, obligation" as in Arabic. *Taklif qilaman* = "I propose / I invite".
**ajoyib** = **WONDERFUL, great** — everyday praise, not "strange" as in Arabic *ʿajīb*.
**gap** = **SPEECH, TALK**, not English *gap*. *Gapiring!* = "speak!"

blocks.text: This course deliberately puts words like these early on. Not to make it easy, but because momentum in the first week decides whether you make it to unit twenty.
These pages aren't for studying — they're for a quick look when you forget a form in the middle of an exercise. Everything here has already been explained step by step in its own unit.
1. Word order (unit 6)

**Subject — Time/place — Object — Verb.** The verb always comes last. *Men ertaga doʻstim bilan bozorga boraman* = "I tomorrow friend-my with bazaar-to go". Question words don't move anything: *Siz qayerga borasiz?* — the verb stays at the end.
2. Predicate endings: an "am/is/are" stuck on the end (unit 1)
The negative uses **emas**, which stands on its own and carries the ending: *Men talaba emasman*. Questions use **-mi**, inserted before the person ending: *Siz talabamisiz?*
3. Six endings that replace prepositions (units 4, 7, 8, 14)

head: Name
Ending

rows: *uyning eshigi* = the door of the house

blocks.text: After **k, q, gʻ** the ending *-ga* hardens: *qishloq* → *qishloqqa*, *togʻ* → *toqqa*, *tok* → *tokka*. Otherwise *-ga* stays *-ga*.
4. Possessive endings (units 3, 14)

The possessive pronoun can be said too, giving a double marking: *mening kitobim*, *sizning uyingiz*, *Anvarning kitobi*. What's required is **the ending on the noun**; the pronoun in front can be dropped.
5. Verbs: four forms are enough for A1

The negative inserts **-ma-** right after the stem: *bormayman* (I don't go), *bormayapman* (I'm not going right now), *bormadim* (I didn't go), *bormoqchi emasman* (I don't intend to go). Stems ending in a vowel use *-y-*: *ishlamoq* → *ishlayman*, *oʻqimoq* → *oʻqiyman*.

blocks.text: 7. Sentences with no "have" (unit 4)

Uzbek has no verb "to have". Owning is expressed as being somewhere: **[owner]-da [thing] bor** = "at X there is Y". *Menda pul bor* = I have money. *Sizda vaqt bormi?* = Do you have time? The negative is *yoʻq*: *Menda pul yoʻq*.
8. The most common function words
These forty verbs cover most everyday conversation. The "I" column uses the habitual form, the "past" column the first-person *-di* form — the two forms you'll need most.

head: Base (-moq)
Meaning
I … (habitual)
I … (past)
rows: to go out; to get on/up

blocks.text: Look at **yoqmoq**: it's the only verb on this list that's almost always used in the third person, because the "doer" is the thing, not you. *Menga palov yoqadi* = "to-me plov is-pleasing" = I like plov. Compare Spanish *me gusta*. The same structure is used for *kerak* (*menga … kerak*) and for pain (*boshim ogʻriyapti*).

If you've reached this page after working through all twenty units, you're on the threshold of A2. You can introduce yourself, ask the way, haggle at the bozor, order a meal, talk about what has happened, and make plans. That's no small thing.
Three things that help most from here:

items: **Learn the second past form (-gan).** This course deliberately uses only *-di*. The *-gan* form — *borganman* (I have been), *koʻrgan odam* (a person who has seen) — is the first door into A2, and it unlocks the whole way Uzbek builds relative clauses.

**Learn verb-building endings.** *Yoz-dir-moq* (to have something written), *koʻr-in-moq* (to be seen, to appear), *yuv-in-moq* (to wash oneself). Uzbek builds new verbs from old ones like Lego, and once you see the pattern, your vocabulary multiplies without memorizing.

**Listen, don't just read.** Look up songs by Sevara Nazarkhan or Yulduz Usmonova, watch the Uzbekistan 24 news channel on YouTube, or put on Oʻzbekiston radio. The alphabet is Latin, so you can follow the lyrics as you read — a luxury learners of Russian or Arabic don't have.

blocks.text: And a note about where it's spoken. Uzbek is used by more than 35 million people in Uzbekistan, plus large communities in northern Afghanistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Kazakhstan. It's also a back door into Turkish, Kazakh, Uyghur, and Turkmen — their structure is nearly identical, and most of this course will carry straight over.

If you'd like to continue with a teacher, Linguo offers private Uzbek classes from A1 to B2. What helps most at this stage isn't more theory but someone who listens to you speak and corrects your *q*, *x*, and *gʻ* before they harden into habits.
*Omad tilayman — koʻrishguncha!*
